newsitem.title: USA: Sewage poses health risks in flooded North Carolina.
newsitem.headline: Sewage poses health risks in flooded North Carolina.

text.p: North Carolina health officials on Friday warned residents to avoid lakes, rivers and flooded areas hard-hit by Hurricane Fran after learning that tons of raw sewage had escaped from damaged treatment systems.
Gov. Jim Hunt, who toured ravaged communities by helicopter, said flooding that followed in the wake of the deadly storm may have caused more damage than the hurricane itself.

The University of North Carolina at Wilmington also issued a preliminary damage report estimating that five coastal counties in the southeastern part of the state may need $13 billion in government aid and insurance proceeds over the next 12 months.
"This is a lot worse than anything I have ever seen," the governor told reporters during his tour of the state.
Vast tracts of land remained under flood waters in southeastern areas around Wilmington, including Columbus, Pender, Onslow and New Hanover counties.

"Rivers and lakes in the eastern part of the state are contaminated with literally tons of raw sewage from more than 80 sewage systems disabled by Hurricane Fran," said Dr. Ron Levine, the state's health director.
"We are urging everyone to avoid contact with streams, lakes or any area where the water is suspect," he said, although no specific health problems were reported.

Hurricane Fran raked through the mid-Atlantic a week ago, eventually killing 39 people and devastating miles of coastline in seven states. About 42 North Carolina counties, or half of the state, were ravaged by the storm.

Part of the sewage problem has been residential septic pipes torn by falling trees. State officials said they also knew of at least three hog farm waste-lagoons that had overflowed, and said they expected to find more.
But the biggest danger has been posed by municipal systems, mostly in the Wake County area, which could no longer contain all the waste flowing into them.

The City of Raleigh's system has released 50 to 70 million gallons of partially treated sewage into Swift Creek and the Neuse River, waterways that ultimately flow into flooded regions near Goldsboro.
